title: High-resolution and bias-corrected CMIP5 projections for climate change impact assessments
problem: Global Climate Model projections are too coarse and biased for direct use in agricultural and biodiversity impact assessments, which require finer-scale, high-resolution climate data to model local-scale impacts.
method: The paper presents a bias-correction and downscaling approach, the delta method, which generates high-resolution future climate projections by applying spatially interpolated climate model anomalies to a high-resolution observed climate baseline for use in impact assessments.
task: The task is to produce a global database of high-resolution, bias-corrected future climate projections from coarse CMIP5 model outputs by applying the delta method, intended for climate change impact assessments on agriculture and biodiversity.

Since no observations of future climate exist, we used one GCM as pseudo-observations, to then try to predict the future evolution of that simulation using another independent simulation (Fig. 4). We selected the GFDL-ESM2M as the reference simulation (the ‘perfect sibling’ or ‘truth’) and compared with the same data from other 5 GCMs in the periods 1960–1990 and 2040–2069. Raw refers to the uncorrected data and DC after applying the bias-correction approach. We assessed the skill using the RMSE between the perfect sibling and the other GCMs.

Fig. 4 Demonstration of the DC calibration methodology using a range of GCM simulations. Top maps (in blue color scale) show results for DJF seasonal rainfall, and bottom maps (in rainbow color scale) for DJF mean seasonal temperature. GFDL-ESM2M is selected as the “prefect sibling” for verification against the calibrated projections using other GCM data. The RMS error for the region shown is given as the E value in the top-right of the maps.
